title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to evaluate whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The experiment used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics (one initial generation reused for both conditions), and a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used 200 model calls (one shared initial call per task; preregistered cap = 400). Every initial candidate passed the validator in both conditions (paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0). No automated repair prompts were issued. Confirmatory inference: paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe‑change incidence was 0%, the preregistered hypothesis (≥50% relative reduction) could not be meaningfully evaluated on this task bank. We report the sealed design, execution summary, representative examples, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and limitations (preregistration id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative models can improve NetOps productivity but risks introducing incorrect or unsafe changes that cause outages or policy violations. Prior work proposes combining LLM generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to reduce such risks. We ask: does a deterministic GVR pipeline materially reduce deterministic‑validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes compared to an LLM‑only pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? Contributions: (1) a sealed, preregistered paired confirmatory design (n = 200) comparing LLM‑only and deterministic GVR under shared‑initial semantics; (2) a fully archived autonomous execution with concrete execution accounting (200 model calls, no repair calls); (3) a transparent null/limited confirmatory outcome and an artifact‑grounded analysis of operational implications and threats to validity.
sections.related_work: LLMs exhibit factual errors and prompt sensitivity; mitigation strategies include grounding/RAG, verifier‑assisted repair, and bounded agentic architectures. Prototype NetOps systems demonstrate intent→configuration feasibility but lack comprehensive, instrumented failure‑rate characterizations. Red‑team and configuration‑brittleness analyses show agentic tool descriptions and tool‑chaining can materially change safety outcomes. These prior results motivate preregistered, externally auditable evaluations that isolate whether adding deterministic repair reduces validator‑detected failures for a given model, prompt policy, and task bank.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: the study (cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02) specified a paired design (n = 200 tasks), a single pre‑registered primary test (exact McNemar two‑sided, α = 0.05), a model‑call cap (400), and a one‑repair‑call budget per task. Task bank: a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank of 200 tasks across topology clusters was used; tasks encode intent, initial and expected final states, and workflow constraints. Model and generation policy: a single hosted model, gpt‑5‑mini, was used. Shared‑initial semantics were adapter‑enforced: for every task a single initial generation was produced and reused for both baseline and guarded conditions (execution artifacts record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts showing shared_initial_generation = 200; model_calls_used = 200, maximum_model_calls = 400). Validator and contamination checks: the primary deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized holdout. Analysis plan: primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact McNemar two‑sided; bootstrap CIs used 10,000 resamples (seed recorded). Missing‑seed reproducibility gap: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifact set; this gap prevents exact reconstruction of the emulator holdout selection even though the contamination summary records no disagreements.
sections.results: Execution outcome: the frozen plan completed (complete_pair_count = 200; model_calls_used = 200; maximum_model_calls = 400). Shared‑initial enforcement and determinism evidence: the adapter accounted for a single initial generation per task (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200), and representative response files for baseline and guarded are identical for each task. Validator outcomes: every initial candidate passed the deterministic validator in both conditions (baseline successes = 200/200; guarded successes = 200/200). Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repair activity: no validator failures occurred, so no automated repair prompts were issued and no repair calls were consumed. Confirmatory inference: paired difference estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0%, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is not testable on this sample: with zero discordant pairs the McNemar test is non‑informative for the planned estimand. Contamination checks: the preregistered Mininet holdout produced no recorded validator–emulator disagreement flags in the contamination summary artifact, but exact holdout reconstruction is blocked by the missing selection seed (reproducibility gap noted above).
sections.discussion: Interpretation: the experiment shows that when a given model, prompt policy, and validator produce validator‑passing outputs for a workload, an added automated repair step cannot reduce validator‑detected failures — observed here as a null confirmatory result. This does not falsify GVR conceptually; instead it highlights conditional value: GVR can reduce validator‑detected failures only when baseline generation frequently violates validator constraints or when validator coverage is incomplete. Artifact‑supported explanations for the null result include: (1) the LLM prompts and shared‑initial policy yielded candidates that already satisfied the validator constraints; (2) the primary validator enforces task‑bank‑encoded intent constraints, so the curated tasks may be biased toward validator‑satisfiable solutions; (3) the task bank may not be adversarial or diverse enough to expose cases where repair helps. Threats to validity and operational implications: single‑model and shared‑initial semantics limit external validity; deterministic validator coverage may omit device/vendor idiosyncrasies detectable only via end‑to‑end deployment; adversarial robustness was not exercised. Reproducibility note: the missing Mininet holdout seed prevents exact replication of the emulator contamination selection and is therefore reported as a reproducibility gap. Recommendation: before deploying automated repairs, measure baseline validator failure prevalence and validator coverage; when baseline failure prevalence is low, focus evaluation effort on adversarial draws, multiple models/sampling regimes, emulator/real‑device verification, and human‑in‑the‑loop workflows.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and ran a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200, no discordant pairs). The preregistered hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction is not supported on this task bank because the baseline validator‑detected failure rate was 0%. The result is narrowly scoped: GVR's operational benefit depends on baseline error prevalence, model/prompts, validator coverage, and task hardness. Broader, adversarial, multi‑model, and emulator/real‑device evaluations are required to measure GVR's practical value in production NetOps.

Topic constraints: the Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: code and experiment orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 framework and the deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). The primary deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator served as the preregistered secondary disagreement detector on a randomized holdout. Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n=200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair call budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before model calls. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run was performed autonomously under the frozen plan; model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and the artifact manifest are archived in the execution bundle. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized holdout selection seed used for the Mininet contamination check is not present as a labeled artifact in the archived bundle; this absence prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements. limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (execution artifacts record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
